If you mean meal-kit subscriptions where ingredients/meal components are delivered and you cook a quick dinner, India is a bit different from the US/UK market. There aren't many strong true meal-kit subscriptions in Bengaluru, so I’d compare meal kits + ready-to-cook/heat-and-eat services rather than force a HelloFresh-style comparison.

My top 3 for two busy vegetarian adults
Option	Best for	Value	Effort	Main trade-off
FreshToHome	Cheapest flexible option	⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐	5–15 min	Not actually a subscription
MealMonk	Zero-cooking convenience in HSR	⭐⭐⭐⭐	~0–5 min	More like prepared meals than meal kits
Vibrant Living	Health/protein-focused vegetarian meals	⭐⭐⭐⭐	~0–5 min	Costs more; less “cook together” experience

1. FreshToHome — best value if you don't need a formal subscription

FreshToHome has a substantial vegetarian/ready-to-cook range, and its ready-to-eat catalogue currently includes things like paneer tikka, Thai veg curry + rice, chole chawal and paneer pulao. Examples currently range roughly from ₹99–₹159 per pack. 
Fresh To Home
+1

The catch: FreshToHome explicitly says it doesn't offer subscriptions, so you'd have to reorder manually. 
Fresh To Home

Why I'd shortlist it: for two people, you can assemble 3–4 dinners/week without committing to a large monthly plan.

2. MealMonk — best if you're in HSR and just want dinner solved

MealMonk is particularly interesting if you're around HSR. It delivers 100% vegetarian home-style meals, cooked fresh daily, with dinner delivery around 7:30–8:30 PM and the ability to pause plans. 
mealmonk.in

This isn't really a conventional meal kit: you aren't cooking. That's actually its advantage if "busy" is the biggest constraint.

3. Vibrant Living — best if nutrition matters

Vibrant Living focuses specifically on vegetarian/protein-oriented meal subscriptions in Bengaluru. Its published comparisons emphasize protein content, macro customization and vegetarian protein sources such as paneer, tofu, lentils and quinoa. 
Vibrant Living
+1

I'd choose this over a generic tiffin service if you're trying to make dinner fit around gym/fitness goals, but I'd verify the actual weekly price and protein numbers before committing.

The trade-offs I'd check before subscribing

1. Price per person, not price per box
For two adults, calculate:

monthly subscription ÷ actual number of individual dinners delivered

A ₹5,000 plan that only covers 12 dinners for two isn't really ₹5,000/month for dinner. It's ₹208/person/meal.

2. Cooking time vs preparation time
There's a big difference between:

2–5 min → heat and eat

10–15 min → assemble/cook

25–40 min → genuine meal kit

For busy professionals, I'd pay slightly more to stay under 15 minutes.

3. Protein
Vegetarian meals can look healthy while being mostly rice/roti + gravy. I'd look for roughly 20–30g protein per dinner, particularly if you're exercising.

4. Portion size
Check whether "serves 2" actually means two adult dinner portions. This is one of the easiest ways for a seemingly cheap service to become expensive.

5. Delivery window
For working late, a fixed 7–8 PM delivery can be annoying. Flexible delivery or chilled meals that you can heat later may be worth paying more for.

6. Skip/pause policy
This matters more than a small introductory discount. Look for no-penalty skips, no minimum long-term commitment and easy cancellation.

My pick

For two busy adults, I'd start with FreshToHome if you actually want to cook, and MealMonk if you mainly want dinner off your plate. I'd only pay the premium for Vibrant Living if its nutrition/protein targets line up with what you're trying to achieve.

ads.prompt: I want to compare options for endpoint security for a 100-person business with remote staff. Which three choices offer the best value, and what trade-offs should I check?
ads.answer:
For a 100-person business with remote staff, I’d shortlist these three:

Option	Best value when	Approx. cost	Main trade-off
Microsoft Defender for Business	You already use Microsoft 365	₹250/user/month standalone	Best value, but less compelling if you need deep cross-platform threat hunting
CrowdStrike Falcon	Security quality is the priority	Around $8/device/month for Falcon Go	More expensive and the SMB tier has a 100-device cap
Sophos Intercept X	You have little/no security team	Quote-based	Strong protection + MDR options, but pricing and management can be more complex
1. Microsoft Defender for Business — my value pick

At ₹250/user/month, 100 users would be about ₹25,000/month or ₹3 lakh/year before GST if bought standalone. It supports Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, includes EDR, vulnerability management and automated investigation/remediation. 
Microsoft
+1

If you're already paying for Microsoft 365 Business Premium, Defender for Business is included, along with Intune, Entra ID and Defender for Office 365. That makes the overall value particularly hard to beat. 
Microsoft

Trade-off: you're getting the best economics if you're Microsoft-centric. For a mixed Windows/macOS/Linux environment or a company wanting very deep threat hunting, I'd look harder at CrowdStrike.

2. CrowdStrike Falcon — best standalone security choice

Falcon Go is currently positioned for 5–100 devices, with published pricing around $59.99/device/year. It gives you a more platform-agnostic EDR approach and a strong upgrade path as your security requirements grow. 
Unió Digital
+1

Trade-off: at exactly 100 devices you're already at the Falcon Go ceiling. Also, MDR/24×7 human monitoring costs extra. So the real TCO can be substantially higher than the headline endpoint price.

3. Sophos Intercept X — best if nobody wants to babysit security

Sophos is particularly worth considering if your 100-person company doesn't have a dedicated security person. Intercept X can be paired with Sophos MDR, giving you human monitoring and response rather than simply handing your IT person another alert dashboard. 
MSP Compared
+1

Trade-off: Sophos pricing is generally quote-based, so comparing the sticker price with Defender or Falcon isn't apples-to-apples. Get the quote with MDR, onboarding, support and renewal pricing explicitly separated.

What I'd check before signing

For a remote 100-person company, I'd weight these more heavily than raw antivirus detection scores:

MDR vs. unmanaged EDR
Who actually responds to an alert at 2 AM? If the answer is "our IT guy will check it tomorrow," pay for MDR.

Remote isolation
Can you immediately isolate a compromised laptop from the internet while keeping the management connection alive?

Off-network protection
Test a laptop that hasn't connected to your corporate VPN for weeks. The endpoint agent should still protect and report it.

macOS coverage
Don't accept "Mac supported" at face value. Check whether the same EDR/response features exist on Windows and Mac.

Employee-owned devices
If staff use personal laptops, clarify exactly what gets installed, what data the company can see, and whether BYOD is actually supported.

Device-count pricing
Ask whether laptops, mobiles, servers and contractors count separately. CrowdStrike's 100-device Falcon Go limit is particularly relevant at your size. 
Unió Digital
+1

Identity + email security
Endpoint protection won't stop everything. For remote workers, MFA, conditional access, phishing protection and device compliance are just as important.

My recommendation

If you're already on Microsoft 365 → Defender for Business.
If you're not Microsoft-centric and want best-in-class standalone EDR → CrowdStrike.
If you don't have security expertise in-house → Sophos + MDR.

For a 100-person startup/SMB, I would not automatically buy the most expensive enterprise EDR. The bigger risk is paying for a sophisticated dashboard that nobody is actually monitoring.

Zoho CRM	Standard	Best value if you want lots of CRM functionality cheaply
🥇 Pipedrive Growth — my pick

For a 5-person sales team, I'd start with Growth, not Essential.

You want the email sync, sales automation and follow-up capabilities rather than buying a cheap plan and discovering that the workflows you actually need are locked behind an upgrade.

Your setup would be:

5 reps → 1 pipeline → Gmail/Outlook sync → automated follow-ups → manager dashboard

You don't need advanced customization initially.

🥈 HubSpot Sales Hub Starter

HubSpot is the better choice if your sales process is going to connect closely with website leads, forms, marketing, customer lifecycle and inbound leads.

Current HubSpot pricing lists Sales Hub Starter from $20/month per seat, although HubSpot's packaging and feature limits vary by product/seat, so check the exact checkout configuration. 
Legal Center

For five seats, that's roughly $100/month before taxes at the listed starting price.

🥉 Zoho CRM Standard

Zoho is surprisingly strong for the money. Its current India pricing shows ₹800/user/month for Standard when billed annually, including email integration, mass emails, multiple pipelines and sales forecasting. Professional is ₹1,400/user/month. 
Zoho

For five people:

Standard ≈ ₹4,000/month

That's excellent value if you're comfortable with a slightly more complex interface.

The hidden costs I'd check before signing

This is actually more important than the headline price.

1. Email automation limits

Ask:

"Does this exact plan include automated multi-step follow-up sequences?"

Not just email integration.

There's a big difference between:

CRM can send emails

and

CRM can automatically send:

Email 1 → wait 3 days → no reply → Email 2 → wait 5 days → Email 3 → create task for salesperson.

That's the functionality I'd make sure is included.

2. Number of users/seats

Check whether:

all 5 salespeople need paid seats

manager/admin seats cost the same

read-only/reporting users are free

automation users count as seats

Don't assume "5-person team" means exactly five paid licenses.

3. Email sending limits

There are usually separate considerations for:

1-to-1 sales emails

automated sequences

bulk/marketing emails

monthly email volume

If you're doing outbound prospecting, don't use a CRM's marketing email system as a substitute for a proper outbound email infrastructure.

4. Reporting limits

Check whether your plan lets you create:

pipeline by salesperson

pipeline by stage

monthly forecast

won/lost analysis

conversion rates

aging/stale deals

activity/follow-up reports

You don't need 100 reports. You need 5–8 useful ones.

5. Automation limits

Check the number of:

workflows

automation runs

sequences

active automations

actions per automation

This is where cheap plans can become frustrating.

6. WhatsApp / calling / third-party integrations

If your team eventually wants WhatsApp, phone calling, LinkedIn, Google Workspace, Slack, etc., check whether those are native or require a paid integration/third-party tool.

Zoho, for example, advertises 1,200+ integrations, which is a genuine advantage if you expect a more connected sales stack. 
Zoho

7. Annual vs monthly pricing

Don't compare:

$14/month

against

$20/month

until you know whether one number assumes annual billing.

I'd calculate the actual 12-month cash cost for five users, including taxes.

What I'd do in your position

I'd run a 14-day side-by-side test with the same 20–30 leads:

Pipedrive Growth vs HubSpot Sales Hub Starter vs Zoho Standard

Give each salesperson the same workflow:

Import 30 leads

Assign owner

Send first email

Schedule follow-up

Move deal through pipeline

Mark lost/won

Manager checks dashboard

Then ask the team one question:

"Which one would you actually keep updated every day?"

For a 5-person team coming from spreadsheets, adoption is more important than having 200 CRM features.

My final ranking: Pipedrive Growth → HubSpot Starter → Zoho Standard.

And if keeping the monthly bill very low matters, Zoho Standard is the value winner at roughly ₹4,000/month for five users based on its current India annual pricing.

ads.answer:
For long days on your feet, I’d prioritize comfort and fatigue reduction over looks. Under ₹6,000, you can get genuinely good options.

What to look for

Cushioning, but not a super-soft “sinking” sole

Look for a cushioned EVA/foam midsole.

A slightly responsive foam is better for 8–12 hours because your feet don't work as hard.

Good heel cushioning

Especially important if you're walking on concrete/tile all day.

Avoid very flat, thin-soled sneakers.

Breathable upper

Mesh is preferable in Bangalore/Indian weather.

Your feet will swell slightly over a long day, so avoid tight synthetic uppers.

Enough toe room

Your toes shouldn't touch the front when walking downhill or after several hours.

Don't automatically size up; look for a naturally wider toe box.

Stable outsole + decent grip

You don't want a shoe that's so soft and flexible that your foot feels unstable.

Rubber sections on the outsole are useful for wet/slippery surfaces.

Weight

For everyday walking, lighter is generally better.

You don't need a heavy "support" shoe unless you specifically need that type of stability.

Fit > brand

Try them later in the day, when your feet are slightly swollen. That's also recommended by podiatry-focused footwear guidance.
